transcript:
Meeting header:
2027-09-29 15:00 PDT · 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Rivera (Redwood SE), Sarah Lee (Aurora Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Aurora CTO), Priya Nair (Aurora Product)

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of Redwood structured output + function/tool calling. Showed JSON mode, schema validation, guardrails and a demo of calling an internal billing tool via function call. Discussed hosting options, perf/cost tradeoffs, and next steps for a pilot.

00:00 Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're going to jump in. Luca and I will run through a short demo of structured output and function calling in Redwood, show how you can get deterministic JSON responses and call out to internal tools.
00:18 Tom (Aurora): Great, we only have 40 minutes so if you can focus on the parts that help with our merchant reconciliation flow that would be awesome.
00:28 Maya: Absolutely — we actually built a small sample around reconciliation, invoice enrichment, and auto-resolution. Luca will start with the API and JSON schema mode.
00:45 Luca (Redwood): Cool, opening my screen — apologies if the screen share lags a bit. So here is the Redwood Console, top nav: Models, Routes, Observability, Optimize. I'll click into an API route we demo'd earlier.
01:10 Luca: For structured output we enable JSON mode, where you provide a schema for the model to follow. We show a sample schema on the right: invoice_id (string), merchant_id (string), amount_cents (integer), currency (string), status enum ["ok","flagged","requires_review"], and a nested suggested_action object with action_type and payload.
01:40 Sarah: Quick Q — nested objects worry us because of hallucination. How strict is this schema enforcement?
01:50 Luca: Good question. In JSON mode we do a combination of constrained decoding plus post-generation validation. The model is biased toward the schema; if the output doesn't validate, Redwood can optionally call the model again, return a structured error, or fall back to a human-in-the-loop flow. We also show a confidence score per field.
02:12 Sarah: So if the amount is off the model will flag instead of returning bad data?
02:18 Luca: Yup, example during the demo: the model returned amount_cents with low confidence and we marked it requires_review.
02:30 Maya: I want to show function calling — think of it as the LLM producing a structured payload that then triggers an internal microservice. In our sample we call an internal billing / resolution API to attempt auto-apply payments.
02:48 Luca: I'll switch to our function-calling sample. The model is asked to produce a call like: {"function":"apply_payment","args":{...}}. Redwood's runtime can execute that function or return the JSON for your backend to call.
03:10 Tom: Is the function executed inside Redwood or do we need to host the function?
03:18 Luca: You have options — Hosted: Redwood can proxy the call to a customer webhook (we don't execute arbitrary code), Dedicated/Private: you can deploy a secure function runner inside your VPC, or you can have Redwood just return the structured payload and your service executes it. For security we recommend signed webhooks + mutual TLS or a VPC connector.
03:45 Priya: For our use case we want the LLM to propose an action but not auto-execute without an approval step. Can the console show a preview?
03:55 Maya: Yes — you can configure a route to return the structured payload and also create a flow in the Console to surface suggested_actions for human approval. We demonstrated a canary rollout where 10% of calls auto-execute and the rest go to review.
04:15 Luca: Now I'm going to run a live query against a sample merchant record. Sending request...
04:32 (transcription noise) Speaker 2: uh-huh
04:35 Luca: Response came back in JSON mode — I'll paste the raw response: {"invoice_id":"inv_20270901_9","merchant_id":"m_423","amount_cents":129900,"currency":"USD","status":"ok","suggested_action":{"action_type":"none","payload":null},"field_confidence":{"amount_cents":0.98}}
04:58 Sarah: Looks good — what's the typical latency on that?
05:05 Luca: For that sample it was ~280ms p50 on the hosted route. If you need sub-100ms we recommend model + hardware tuning on Dedicated with batching disabled for low latency.
05:20 Sarah: And cost? We're processing millions of events a month.
05:25 Maya: Redwood Optimize gives quantization and batching recommendations per workload. For high-throughput event processing you can use a cheaper quantized model with batching and caching; for per-request strict latency we suggest a higher perf instance with reserved capacity. We'll send a TCO.
05:44 Tom: We have strict data residency and SOC2 requirements. How do logs and payloads behave?
05:52 Luca: In Private mode you can keep everything inside your VPC. We support KMS-backed encryption for at-rest, envelope encryption for KV cache, and audit logs with configurable retention. For hosted customers we offer SOC2 controls, SSO/SAML, RBAC and field-level redaction options.
06:20 Priya: For guardrails can we enforce allowed actions? For example, don't allow refunds above $10k without manual review.
06:30 Maya: Yes — you can include guardrail rules in the routing policy or as schema-level validation. The Console lets you define post-processing policies: threshold checks, blocklist/allowlist, and automatic label for a manual review queue.
06:45 Sarah: Can we integrate this into our existing orchestration — Airflow and our ticketing system?
06:52 Luca: Absolutely — function calls are simple HTTP webhooks; typical integration is model returns a suggested_action payload and we POST it to your orchestration endpoint. We also support structured output webhooks where we sign payloads.
07:10 (short crosstalk)
07:20 Luca: I'm going to show the Console Observability tab — token-level cost, latency breakdown per model, and an example Optimize run which suggested switching to q4_0 quantized model for lower token cost with a small delta in accuracy. You can preview the estimated monthly savings.
07:45 Priya: Is there an automatic rollback if the accuracy drops?
07:50 Maya: Yes, you can configure automatic regression detection tied to a prompt set — if quality degrades beyond a threshold the route rolls back to the previous model.
08:05 Luca: Back to function calling — I'll simulate a mis-structured output to show validation. Sending a deliberately ambiguous prompt...
08:25 Luca: The model produced a bad type for amount_cents (string instead of integer). Console shows a validation error. We have three options: re-call model with stricter decoding, return a structured error, or mark for review.
08:42 Sarah: In practice, what percent of calls need a re-call?
08:47 Luca: It depends on schema complexity and prompt engineering — for typical invoice extraction we see 95% schema-valid on first try with the schema bias. Complex nested payloads are the main failure mode.
09:05 Tom: For the pilot we want to measure both precision/recall on parsed fields and the operational cost.
09:12 Maya: We'll include a benchmarking plan — we'll run parallel inference on your sample events and compare hosted vs dedicated latency and cost.
09:25 (30s pause as Luca sets up next demo)
09:55 Luca: Now I'm going to demo tool chaining — the model can call multiple functions in sequence. Example: parse invoice -> look up merchant risk profile -> propose action. Each function call is captured in the trace and you can see timings in Observability.
10:20 Priya: Nice, that trace visibility is helpful for debugging whoops.
10:28 Luca: Here's an example trace: parse_invoice (120ms) -> merchant_lookup (40ms) -> propose_action (75ms). Total runtime depends on whether calls are proxied or executed internally.
10:42 Sarah: Any rate limits on function calls?
10:46 Maya: We offer configurable rate limits per route and token-level quotas. For Dedicated customers you can also set autoscaling policies and burst capacity.
11:00 Tom: How are secrets handled in function calls? We don't want API keys floating around in logs.
11:06 Luca: Secrets are stored in the customer's key vault (we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp) and never logged in plaintext. When Redwood proxies to a webhook we inject a short-lived signed token.
11:22 Sarah: Could you show an example of schema + guardrail for refunds?
11:28 Luca: Sure — I'll paste the schema and a short guardrail rule. (typing) guardrail: if suggested_action.action_type == "refund" AND payload.amount_cents > 1000000 then set status = "requires_review" and add tag = "high_value_refund". The Console will surface these automatically.
12:05 Tom: That helps. For compliance we may want to snapshot request/response pairs for audits. How long do you retain those?
12:12 Maya: Retention is configurable per account; hosted default is 90 days, enterprise customers can opt for longer retention or forward logs to their own S3/GCS for indefinite storage. We'll include retention options in the docs we send.
12:30 (slight inaudible section)
12:50 Luca: I'm going to run a quick end-to-end with the merchant dataset you shared (redacted). Sending...
13:12 Luca: Response shows 3 flagged invoices out of 50 and 47 ok. I'll open one of the flagged results — note the suggested_action payload includes an explanation string and field_confidence for auditability.
13:38 Sarah: The explanation is great for our reconciliation team — do you provide a formatted human-readable summary?
13:45 Luca: Yes, we can generate a short natural language explanation alongside the structured payload or store it as part of the trace to be surfaced in your UI.
14:02 Priya: From product perspective we need to map these outputs into our ticketing system — can we customize mapping rules?
14:10 Maya: You can map using post-processing hooks in Redwood or in your own middleware; we also provide a rules engine in Console for simple mappings.
14:30 Tom: Any concerns about PII — merchant data includes banking references.
14:36 Luca: We recommend field-level redaction in the ingestion pipeline and using Private mode if you need on-prem guarantees. For hosted we can redact or hash fields before storing.
14:50 (brief cross-talk, someone drops for a second)
15:05 Maya: Quick note on SDKs — we have JS, Python, and a lightweight golang client. SDK will do structured validation client-side if you want to guard earlier.
15:20 Sarah: Good, our stack is mostly Python with some Node.
15:25 Luca: I'll show Optimize suggestions for this workload — Optimize flagged that using prefix caching for merchant history reduces tokens by ~30% and latency by ~15% for repeated queries.
15:42 Tom: That seems impactful for cost.
15:48 Maya: Ok, time for a short recap and next steps.
15:54 Maya: Recap: Redwood can produce deterministic JSON outputs with schema enforcement, optionally execute function calls or return payloads for your services, provide guardrails for finance rules, and surface observability and Optimize recommendations. We will run a pilot benchmark and send pricing + docs.
16:15 Sarah: Sounds good. We'll prepare a small sample and confirm access to a staging webhook for the function proxy test.
16:22 Priya: Also please include an example mapping from suggested_action to our Jira/GitHub tickets.
16:28 Maya: Got it — we'll include mapping examples and a short playbook for approval flows.
16:36 Tom: One last question — can we do an on-prem pilot?
16:40 Maya: Yes, Private deployment is possible; it takes more lead time for on-site network setup but gives you full control over keys and logs. We'll include an onboarding checklist.
16:52 Luca: I'm pasting links in chat: demo recording, JSON schema examples, security whitepaper, and a sample benchmark spreadsheet.
17:05 (link paste noise)
17:12 Maya: Thanks everybody — we'll follow up with action items.
17:18 (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional mis-attrs (Speaker 2), minor punctuation/word swap errors, some inaudible sections preserved as short notes.

End of transcript.
